newsitem.title: JAPAN: Hedge funds leave Japan bond market in chaos.
newsitem.headline: Hedge funds leave Japan bond market in chaos.

text.p: Recent U.S. hedge funds' aggressive short-squeezing has left the Japanese government bond (JGB) market in chaos, overshadowing the future of the market's new settlement system due to start next month.
Many market players said the funds' activity pushed some market participants to the verge of failing to deliver necessary cash JGBs at settlement, which has never before happened.
Failure to deliver bonds is strictly forbidden in Japan's settlement system, unlike many other countries where failure is overlooked if a fine is paid.

The hedge funds' activity centred around the September JGB futures and the cheapest cash JGBs deliverable against the September contract, namely the 161st and the 163rd 10-year JGBs. Cash delivery for the September is due on Friday.
A record 2.3519 trillion yen ($21.5 billion) worth of the September contract is due for settlement through delivery of cash JGBs, according to the Tokyo Stock Exchange (TSE).
Some said those funds would receive about 1.8 trillion yen ($16.5 billion) worth or about three-fourths of the total JGBs to be delivered.
Many traders said CS First Boston Ltd seems to be receiving much of the cash delivery against the September contract, trading on behalf of the hedge funds.
One official at CS First Boston said he was aware of such market talk but declined to comment, citing client confidentiality.

While the hedge funds are said to have huge long positions in the 161st and the 163rd JGBs through cash delivery of the September contract, they have been borrowing an enormous amount of the same JGBs, bond traders said.
Some traders said the funds have borrowed about 500 billion yen ($4.58 billion) worth of the 161st JGBs, and the same amount of the 163rd JGBs.
As the outstanding amount of these two JGBs are about 700 billion yen ($6.42 billion) each, the hedge funds have a virtual monopoly over them, some traders said.

Reflecting an extreme shortage of these JGBs, their repo rates (lending fees) have shot up in the last couple of weeks. Some said the repo rate for the 161st JGBs went over 30 percent of the face value in the offshore market, compared with 0.2-0.3 percent about a month ago.

Some dealers complained the recent movement in the market was close to manipulation, as those who amassed and hoarded the cheapest JGBs were lending these bonds to helpless market players who were short of them, at extremely high rates.
They said this kind of activity could have been illegal if it had been in the United States.

The whole incident also highlighted the lack of liquidity of the JGB market, dealers said. "Some people might have placed too much trust in the liquidity of the JGB market," said a dealer at a Japanese bank.

The lack of liquidity is a serious problem particularly at a time when the market is launching the rolling settlement system, said Yoshiki Fujioka, manager of the Yen Bond Derivative Department at Credit Lyonnais.
The JGB market on Thursday began rolling settlement, called T plus seven, in which every transaction is settled seven business days after trading from October.
Those who go short in specific bonds have to borrow them on the repo market and therefore liquidity of the repo market is a prerequisite for smooth settlement, traders said.
Up until Wednesday, cash JGBs trading was settled once every five days. Thursday marks the first day of the new system, with dealing on Thursday settled on October 1. ($1-109 yen)
